g.text: Contents
Talk
History
A four-stroke engine is a kind of piston engine in which each piston
completes its work in four separate strokes while the crankshaft turns
twice. It is the design found in most cars, lawn mowers and generators.
Overview
Fuel and air are drawn into a cylinder, squeezed, burnt and then pushed
out again. A valve opens and closes each passage at the right moment,
worked by a camshaft that turns at half the speed of the crankshaft.
The cycle
The piston is joined to the crankshaft by a connecting rod, which turns
its up and down motion into rotation. The four strokes are intake,
compression, power and exhaust, and together they make up one cycle.
History
Engines working on this principle were built in the second half of the
nineteenth century and have been refined ever since, with better fuel
control, lighter parts and cleaner exhaust.
Variations
Some engines use two or more cylinders sharing one crankshaft, and some
replace the spark with compression alone, as in a diesel.
